items.prompt: The document boasts it has exactly two primitives (physics and, when invoked, a normative relation) and no predicate that secretly means 'explains', 'represents', 'is a cause', or 'is knowledge'. Hunt for hidden primitives. Look especially at: 'active commitments', 'declared scope', 'nontrivial binding construction', 'content-preserving recoding', 'grain', 'Org_l(o)', 'relevant', 'the obligation', 'ProducedBy', 'owned'. For each candidate, show whether it is derived from the two primitives and declared indices or is smuggled.

Check every one of Derivations 1 through 10 as a mathematician would. For each: are the stated assumptions sufficient for the conclusion; is any step circular or vacuous; does the 'Consequence' paragraph claim more than the proof gives. Be especially hard on Derivation 1 (kind preservation is a theorem), Derivation 2 (indistinguishable is identical), Derivation 3 (underdetermination), and Derivation 5 (question-finding is representable).

Attack point (A) in 'Where to attack this': construct, as concretely as you can, a candidate that satisfies all four conditions of Account (F1, F2, A, non-circular dependence, non-vacuity) on a physically admitted contract with a non-declared transport, and that plainly provides no explanatory account. Then state whether the document has a reply, quoting it, and whether the reply works.

Attack point (B): produce a genuine explanation whose organization no transport satisfying component fidelity can capture under any physically admitted contract. Focus on eliminative explanation ('why is there no X-effect'), non-causal explanation (mathematical why-questions, symmetry explanations, statistical/selection-artefact explanations), and explanations that work by changing the question. Quote the document's treatment in Part VII and say exactly where it fails if it does.

Attack point (C): the document claims (Part II, Derivation 1) that a kind is nothing over and above an edit-signature, so a declared kind-label can never do discriminating work that admitted changes cannot. Find a case where it can. Consider: historical explanation where no change is available; dispositional properties; cases where the contract is fixed by the question and two genuinely different mechanisms are indistinguishable on it; cases where kinds are individuated by their causal history rather than their forward response. Is 'they are one kind at that contract' an answer or an evasion?

Attack points (D) and (E). (D): Is the three-way provenance distinction (selected / constructed / declared) well-defined? Can every construction witness be rewritten as a selection history plus a relabelling? Is 'no member of the history represents t, H, or the survival condition' checkable, and is 'represents' here itself dependent on (R), making the definition circular? (E): does treating a contract as a content that can be Built trivialise creativity (every re-parameterisation becomes a 'found question') or fail to capture real question-finding?

Steelman the position the document rejects: that an explanation's components must correspond IN KIND to the world's components (an anchoring condition), as an extra condition beyond change-fidelity. What does the document lose by dropping it? Consider: explanations that are correct at a contract but anchored to the wrong mechanism; the pole-and-shadow case when the production contract is unavailable; scientific realism about mechanisms. Then say whether the document's 'Why there is no anchoring condition' section answers you, quoting it.

Find internal contradictions or tensions between parts of the document. Candidates: Part IV says representation requires a selected or constructed transport, but Part V lets an assessment use a declared transport; the 'frozen assessment vs moving question' resolution in Derivation 7; the treatment of grain as a declared index versus the claim that kinds are contract-relative; the claim that (EK) is 'factive about the claimed repair' versus fallibilism; 'Grievance 4' on objectivity versus the contract-relativity of every claim.

Find confounds in the experimental design and result interpretation. In particular: is the 'neutral' one-thing world actually neutral, or does it merely lack the events that would separate the architectures — and is that the same thing? Does 'the τ family ties exactly' establish 'persistence is not selected for', or only that this fitness function cannot see it? Is the exposure/evaluation split by configuration index a real generalisation test given that many configurations share sensory sub-sequences? Does the sensory ceiling comparison do any work?

Section 9 records 21 changes made before freezing. Audit each one: did it change what any pre-registered outcome MEANS, or only how the machinery works? Which changes were made after seeing results that pointed in a particular direction? Is change 16 (the neutrality check 'compared the wrong pair') a legitimate correction or a redefinition to make a failing check pass? Is change 18 (dropping the 0.95 threshold) justified by the stated diagnosis or convenient? Be adversarial but fair: say which changes you would have accepted as a referee.

Read this code as a reviewer hunting for bugs that could produce the reported results spuriously. The reported results: on a one-thing world with no occlusion, persistence values tau=0,2,5,inf tie exactly; on a two-thing world with occlusion, tau=inf uniquely wins; the tau=inf architecture passes the 'thing_signature' test on 100% of bound pairs. Look for: off-by-one in scoring window; the reconcile logic favouring one tau by accident; thing_signature establishing bindings in a way that guarantees passing; the exposure/evaluation split leaking; the sensory ceiling computed on the wrong set; the lookup 'longest available prefix' being unfair to lookups; any place where the tie among tau values is a mathematical necessity of the code rather than a finding.

Argue that the headline result — 'history determined which kind got expressed' — is trivial: a parameter that only matters under occlusion is only selected under occlusion. Then argue the opposite: that the result is non-trivial because of X. Which argument is stronger, and does the results document's section 7 (post-hoc observations) rescue non-triviality or is it post-hoc storytelling?

The 'thing-signature' (M3) test binds slots to things by matching (cell, velocity) at step 2, applies a TRANSLATED edit directly to the slot state, then checks tracking. Argue that this test is circular or trivially passed: the translation already puts the slot where the thing is; the binding is established by the very match it then tests; 'given bound' conditioning throws away the failures. Then say whether the design's defence (that this is component-fidelity F1 computed directly) survives.

Section 1 says the scramble test 'is the test that distinguishes the provenances'. Argue that it is trivial: process C reads defect records and process B does not, BY CONSTRUCTION, so of course scrambling the records breaks C and not B — this tests the code's data flow, not anything about construction versus selection. What would a non-trivial version look like? Does the design have one?

Process C is said to 'never compute an aggregate fitness'. But it scores conditions by (defects covered − non-defects covered) and actions by (defects fixed − non-defects broken). Argue that this IS fitness, itemised, and that the claimed distinction between C and B collapses to 'exhaustive-ish informed search vs mutation search'. Is there any sense in which C 'operates on a representation of the defect' that B does not, beyond efficiency?

Section 1 concedes the regress ('the meta-grammar is fixed; the regress is not escaped'). Argue that this concession guts the experiment: if construction is just 'selection one level up', then 'construction extends what is latent' is either false or vacuous. What would the design have to show to make 'the object grammar grew' a substantive rather than bookkeeping claim? Does it show it?

The rule language contains the action swap_next_v ('take the other's outgoing velocity') and terms n_i, w_i (the slot's own kinematic next-state), and section 12 change 3 redefined the WORLD to be 'kinematics, then a pairwise rule on the kinematic next-states — the same shape as the rule language'. Argue that the world was tailored to the language (or vice versa) so that construction is guaranteed to succeed. Is the defence — that the language is general and the blind search has the same actions — adequate?

Section 12 change 2 adds a pre-registered expectation ('C will not build the crossing rule because crossings are sensorily invisible') after the author 'thought the world through' but before running. Change 4 splits the closedness check after the old grammar's lookup scored 0.819. Audit both: legitimate pre-registration, or post-hoc rationalisation dressed as pre-registration? What is the principled line between 'thinking it through before running' and 'adjusting after seeing results'?

Audit the results document against its own design. Does the 'answer in one paragraph' overclaim relative to the tables? Is 'same machinery, two routes, and the route is detectable by ablation' actually established, or does it follow trivially from how C and B were coded? Is classifying S6 and S7 as 'one clause failed' honest, or should they be marked failed outright? Is the phase-2 confound (contradictory law) a legitimate excuse or a convenient one?

Read this code hunting for bugs that could make the reported construction result spurious. Reported: C builds exactly 'IF n_i == n_j THEN swap_next_v + hold' with fixed=820 broken=0 and stops; scrambling outcomes drops collision fidelity from 0.906 to 0.355; B is byte-identical under the scramble; M6(ii) builds a no-op rule. Look at: collect_records vs construct_round consistency (state after existing rules; the held set); cond_true_any_order vs apply_rules first-match semantics mismatch; predict_with_new_rule merging held sets; whether the exposure/evaluation split leaks through enumerate_configurations_distinct ordering; whether world_step and term_values use the same kinematics so the law is expressible by construction; thing_signature binding logic; whether B's fitness is really exposure-only.

Section 5 of the results says the scramble test 'is not a claim about the code's data flow — it is a demonstration that the two processes' outputs depend on different things'. Attack this. Is there any reading under which the scramble test tells us something about construction versus selection AS CONCEPTS rather than about these two programs? What would the author have to add to make it more than a demonstration that C reads V and B does not?

Section 10 lists 19 failure modes. Find the ones it MISSED. Consider: the constructor's condition scoring (tp - fp) ignoring base rates; top_m=20 truncation; the exposure half being used for both records and rule acceptance with no held-out check inside C; the 'given bound' figures; whether the crossing-invisibility result could be an artefact of how M3 assigns bindings; what happens with 3 slots; whether the ceiling is meaningful for the scramble comparison; the 'byte-identical' B test being trivially true. Rank the missed ones by severity.

The 'invisible law' finding (F3): C never builds the crossing rule because two things bouncing and two things passing through produce identical sensory fields; the M3 test then shows the gap. Argue that this is (a) a genuine, interesting result about contracts and kinds, or (b) a triviality dressed up (of course a learner cannot learn what it cannot observe), or (c) a sign that the sensory contract was chosen to make C look good on everything it could see. Which, and why?

C is a version-space learner: induce a condition from positives vs negatives, solve an action by counterexamples. B is mutation-selection. Both are search. The document claims a difference in 'route', operationalised by the scramble ablation. Argue that the honest conclusion is 'informed search vs blind search differ in what they depend on, and nothing about creativity or explanation follows'. Then say what, if anything, in the results resists that deflation.

Phase 2 is declared confounded because the sticky wall contradicts the reflecting wall. Design a phase-2 replacement law that genuinely EXTENDS the world (is consistent with all existing laws) and that the rule language can express, and state what result would show 'what was built became latent' and what would show it did not. Then say whether the original phase 2 is salvageable by reinterpretation or must be rerun.

Does the construction experiment actually test anything in the semantics document? Map each phase-1 outcome (S1-S6) to the specific definition or derivation in file 10 it is supposed to bear on (Part IV three provenances; the reason-use witness in Part IX; Build in Part X; Derivation 3; Derivation 5). For each, say whether the experiment's operationalisation is faithful to the definition or a loose analogy. Where it is loose, say what a faithful test would require.
